title: The First Rule: Things Keep Going

t: Push a ball. It rolls. Stop pushing. Why does it keep going?
You push a ball, then let go. It keeps moving. What is carrying it?
A ball is pushed and released. It continues moving. Nothing is in contact with it. What keeps it going?
An object given an initial velocity continues in the absence of net force. Why does this need a law?
sub: Nothing is pushing it anymore. So why does it not stop?
For two thousand years people thought things needed a push to keep moving. They were wrong.
Aristotle held that motion requires a continuous cause. Galileo and Newton showed the opposite: a cause is required to STOP motion, not sustain it.
The principle of inertia contradicts the Aristotelian intuition that sustained motion requires sustained force. The first law formalises the correction.

question: In space, with no friction, you push a ball once. What happens?
You push a ball once in space — no air, no friction. What happens to it?
A ball is given an impulse in vacuum, far from any mass. What is its subsequent motion?
An object receives an impulse in a region of negligible net force. Describe its trajectory.
options: It keeps going forever at the same speed
It slows down and stops, just slowly
It speeds up because nothing is holding it back
stages.outcome: It keeps going forever at the same speed
note: This is the answer that took humanity two thousand years to accept. Guess what you think.
Predict before checking. Most people's intuition is wrong here — that intuition is Aristotle's, and it is two thousand years old.
Form a hypothesis. Consider what force, if any, acts on the ball after the impulse.
Predict. Apply the principle of inertia: with no net force, velocity is constant.

t: Set friction to zero. Push the trolley once, then watch — it does not stop.
Set the ground to smooth (friction 0). Launch the trolley. With nothing to slow it, it keeps going.
goal: Reach the goal speed. With no friction, the trolley does not slow down — that is inertia.
Reach the target velocity. In the absence of friction, v is constant — Newton's first law.

t: Set friction to zero and find the smallest push that reaches the goal. Then double the mass — what changes?
With friction = 0, determine the minimum push to reach the goal speed. Then double the mass and predict the new minimum before testing. What does that tell you about inertia vs. force?
goal: Reach the goal. The trolley keeps going — nothing slows it. That is the first law.
Reach the target v. Confirm v is constant under zero net force, regardless of mass.

t: Things keep going unless something stops them. That is called inertia.
Things keep moving unless a force stops them. That is inertia — Newton's first law.
Newton's first law: an object's velocity stays constant unless a net force acts on it. This tendency is called inertia.
Newton's first law (the principle of inertia): in an inertial frame, an object's velocity is constant unless acted on by a net external force. Equivalent to the assertion that inertial frames exist.
sub: More mass means more inertia — heavier things are harder to get moving, and harder to stop.
Mass is the measure of inertia. A heavy trolley needs more push to start, and more force to stop.
Inertia is resistance to changes in motion. Mass quantifies it: F = ma, so larger m means smaller a for the same F.
Mass is the inertial measure. The first law defines inertial frames; the second law (F=ma) quantifies inertia within them.

t: When a car stops suddenly, you keep going forward. That is inertia — the seatbelt is the force that stops you.
A car brakes. Your body keeps moving forward. That is inertia. The seatbelt is the force that stops you.
Whiplash, seatbelt injuries, head impacts in crashes — all inertia. Your body's velocity is unchanged until a force acts.
Inertial reference frames and the first law underlie crash dynamics. A 30 mph delta-v without restraint is fatal because no force decelerates the occupant's organs.

q: In space, with no forces at all, you push a ball once. What happens?
A ball in vacuum receives one push. No forces act afterward. What happens?
An object in a force-free region is given an impulse. Describe its subsequent motion.
In the absence of net external force, what is the trajectory of a body given an initial impulse?
options: It keeps moving at the same speed in a straight line, forever
It slows down and eventually stops
It speeds up because nothing holds it back
why: Nothing is pushing against it. With no force to slow it, the ball keeps its speed. That is inertia — things keep going unless a force stops them.
With no net force, the ball's velocity stays constant (Newton's first law). It does not need a push to keep moving — it needs a force to stop.
Newton's first law: in the absence of net force, velocity is constant. The ball moves in a straight line at constant speed indefinitely.
F_net = 0 ⟹ dv/dt = 0 ⟹ v = const. The principle of inertia. The ball follows a geodesic of flat spacetime — a straight line at constant velocity.

q: Which is harder to get moving — a heavy trolley or a light one?
Which needs more push to start — a heavy trolley or a light one?
Which has more inertia — a 10 kg trolley or a 1 kg trolley?
Which body has greater resistance to acceleration — 10 kg or 1 kg?
options: The heavy one — more mass means more inertia
The light one — it is easier to push
They are the same — inertia does not depend on mass
why: Heavier things are harder to get moving. That is what mass IS — the measure of how hard it is to change something's motion.
Mass is the measure of inertia. A heavy trolley needs more force to achieve the same acceleration (F = ma).
Inertia is proportional to mass. F = ma means a = F/m — larger m gives smaller a for the same F.
Inertial mass quantifies resistance to acceleration: a = F/m. The 10 kg trolley has ten times the inertia of the 1 kg one.
